title: Writing for Rich versus the educational market
summary: Charts for Rich were too hard for college and high school bands, so publishers' grade levels did not fit.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I wonder if you had a feeling and other composer/arrangers have this feeling that I’m writing this chart for Buddy Rich but I want it to be something that other bands will want to play or that I can market to the educational field, and how do I walk that line?

I couldn’t think that way because the stuff that I’d write for Buddy Rich would be too hard for college bands and high school bands to play. And there really wasn’t a market for real professional charts. So when you talk about Hal Leonard or Kendor or any of the publishing companies, they had a level of proficiency that they stuck with for colleges and for high schools. A grade level. Now some of the things that I ended up publishing were kind of scaled down for that market, when I finally did decide to start selling them in the, you know, educational field. But I always, when I was writing for the band I was writing for that band, I wasn’t going to short-change it and try and water it down so it had a second level of, you know, commerciality.
